newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel to begin Jerusalem settlement next week.
newsitem.headline: Israel to begin Jerusalem settlement next week.

text.p: Israel vowed on Friday to break the ground for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem next week, ignoring world pleas to ditch the project which could bring a Palestinian backlash.
The cabinet reaffirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decision to send the bulldozers to a pine-covered hill between East Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
"There is no specific day but it will begin next week," Netanyahu's adviser David Bar-Illan told Reuters.
Palestinian Minister Hanan Ashrawi called the decision foolhardy and said she expected Palestinians to protest peacefully.
The cabinet met as Israel still reeled from the killing of seven schoolgirls on a Jordan Valley field trip by a Jordanian soldier.
"All the ministers were unanimous in urging that work begin as planned this coming week," Bar-Illan said.
He declined to say when construction would start but political sources believe building at the site, called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic, will begin by Monday.
Opposition parties postponed a "no-confidence" debate in parliament due to have been held on Monday over the project while Israel mourned the seven schoolgirls.

Netanyahu pressed ahead with the plan under pressure from the right-wing and Jewish settler groups in his centre-right coaltion government. The decision plunged Israeli-Arab ties to their lowest point since the 1993 Palestinian-Israeli peace accord and angered Western states.

"If anyone thinks the murder of little girls will bring this people to its knees...or that we will relinquish our birthright, holy land and eternal capital, he does not know the strength that exists in each person standing here around me today and in the entire nation," Netanyahu said at a funeral for four of the girls on Thursday night.
The slaughter of the seven girls by a lone Jordanian soldier diverted much of the international criticism Netanyahu has faced over the plan to build 6,500 houses.
"I am building Har Homa this week and nothing is going to stop me," Netanyahu said in an interview with the Maariv newspaper published on Friday.
"If they think they can frighten us, they are mistaken. I am determined about my view more than ever," he said.
The U.N. General Assembly, by a vote of 130 to two, with two abstentions, called on Israel on Thursday to abandon the planned settlement.

The United States and Israel cast the only negative votes on the resolution, similar to one vetoed by the United States in the Security Council on March 7. The Foreign Ministry rejected the resolution as "unilateral" and "useless".
Ashrawi said the decision undermined the peace process.
"This is a very foolhardy decision," she told Reuters.

Asked about fears of violence she said: "I am sure Palestinians will protest and do what is possible to protect their own lands. We know that the protest will be peaceful and hope that the Israelis will not respond with armed violence."

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat went ahead on Friday with plans to receive U.S., European and Arab envoys in Gaza on Saturday to discuss Netanyahu's action which he believes could torpedo the entire U.S.-sponsored peace process.
Arafat, who had shunned contact with Netanyahu, said on Friday he would meet the Israeli leader to discuss settlement.
"If he is ready to implement the agreements, why not?" Arafat told reporters.
Jordan's King Hussein also accused Netanyahu this week of dragging regional peace to the abyss in a private letter which was leaked to the Israeli press.
The king was visibly shocked by the killing on Thursday. He said he wanted to visit the families of the girls, aged 12 to 13, killed at a border site nicknamed "The Island of Peace".
Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak told Reuters on Friday that Israel was checking the possibility of an Arafat meeting and a visit by King Hussein but "nothing has been set".
